classification.tone: Gritty, heightened, operatic, and gruesomely mythic

evaluation.positioning_hook: A blood-soaked Wyoming frontier saga where a mining family’s land war collides with an immortal predator, and every bargain comes due at sundown.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The script has a very legible commercial promise: frontier violence, supernatural menace, and a family-versus-empire conflict that can play to genre audiences immediately. The opening spider attack, the town-wide death event, and the vampire reveal give it the kind of escalation that can generate strong word-of-mouth.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early and cleanly: a Wyoming mining town is built on a supernatural secret, and the people trying to control it are not entirely human. The pilot keeps the engine visible through the mine, the town, the Davenport family, and the full-moon rules, so the viewer always knows what kind of danger is in play.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Abraham, Jane, Jacob, Buddy, and Zoma all arrive with strong behavioral signatures and clear contradictions: pious men with violence in them, a family man who becomes a monster, and a drifter whose deadpan menace gives the show a spine. The ensemble is built for ongoing conflict because every major relationship is also a power struggle.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits hard to a singular frontier nightmare: giant spiders, occult mining, canaries as danger detectors, blood rituals, and a vampire town hierarchy. The tonal confidence is especially notable in how it moves from mythic western to body-horror to darkly comic menace without losing its identity.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The pilot is built like a pressure cooker. It opens with a survival set piece, jumps forward into a town-scale conflict, then keeps layering threats until the final reveal of Jane and Zoma resets the board for series continuation. The ending is a genuine hook because it leaves the audience with a transformed protagonist and a new power dynamic.

resonant_originality.reasoning: This feels like a frontier story that has been metabolized through horror mythology rather than decorated with it. The mine as a literal underworld, the town as a feeding ground, and the vampire family as a corrupt ruling class create an idea that feels both fresh and immediately playable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is full of story-generating details: mining operations, tunnel six, canaries, black powder, town politics, bounty culture, religious language, and a hidden supernatural economy. The setting is not just scenic; it is the mechanism by which the horror and the power structure operate.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very identifiable flavor: biblical dread, western fatalism, and grotesque supernatural spectacle, all delivered with a straight face and sharp, often wicked dialogue. Scenes like the barber-shop standoff, the mine collapse, and the vampire dinner table give it a signature tone that would be hard to mistake for anything else.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the immediate monster-movie surface, the script is setting up family fracture, faith versus corruption, labor exploitation, and the moral cost of survival. The recurring symbols — gold, blood, mirrors, wolves, spiders, and scripture-adjacent language — suggest a larger mythology that can deepen over time.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The pilot is relationship-rich: Abraham/Jane, Abraham/Jacob, Jacob/Buddy, Buddy/Gus, Jane/Zoma, and the town’s various power pairings all generate conflict on contact. The ensemble is not decorative; it is the engine, with every conversation carrying leverage, threat, or betrayal.

casting_characteristics: Twin brothers in the opening sequence
Several roles with specific ethnic/language requirements
Supernaturally ageless or physically imposing antagonist types

technical.vfx_details: Spider creatures, supernatural death effects, bird-fall event, regenerative vampire wounds, and large-scale cavern menace will likely use a mix of practical and digital enhancement.
technical.sfx_needs: Blood effects, creature attacks, explosions, collapses, gunshot hits, and practical gore-heavy transformations.

rights_flags.detail: Historical references to Colonel Canby and General Sibley
No prominent contemporary brand names identified
No obvious external IP dependency identified

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Serialized supernatural western with a town-scale mythology engine, family power struggles, and episodic monster/occult escalation

strengths.what_it_means: The script gives producers a clean, pitchable lane: a frontier town where mining wealth, family ambition, and vampiric power are all the same system. That makes the show easy to market and easy to sustain because every episode can mine both human and supernatural conflict.
strengths.evidence: The mine, the town, the Davenport family, and the vampire reveal all connect into one governing conflict.

strengths.what_it_means: Buddy, the Triplets, the Butler, and Zoma create a villain ecosystem rather than a single bad guy. That gives the series a hierarchy of menace, which is valuable for serialization because it supports shifting alliances, betrayals, and escalating reveals.
strengths.evidence: Buddy’s dinner-table dominance, the Triplets’ ritualized intimacy, the Butler’s quiet authority, and Zoma’s roaming menace all feel like parts of one larger machine.

strengths.what_it_means: Abraham and Jane are built as showcase parts: emotionally legible, morally pressured, and forced into extreme action. Zoma is the kind of charismatic, dangerous wildcard that can become a breakout role if cast right.
strengths.evidence: Abraham’s guilt and stubbornness, Jane’s survival turn, and Zoma’s deadpan, shape-shifting menace all land clearly on the page.

strengths.what_it_means: This has a voice. The dialogue is formal, profane, and mythic all at once, which gives the show a signature that can separate it from standard westerns or standard vampire stories.
strengths.evidence: The barber-shop standoff, the mine speeches, and the dinner confrontation all use elevated frontier language with a nasty edge.

strengths.what_it_means: The pilot is packed with images that sell in a trailer: giant spiders, a collapsing cave, birds dropping from the sky, a blood ritual dinner, and a town emptied by supernatural death. That is valuable for both buyer interest and audience recall.
strengths.evidence: The spider attack, the cavern collapse, the bird-fall sequence, and the vampire reveal are all highly visual and cinematic.

strengths.what_it_means: The script establishes practical supernatural logic — moonlight, blood, silver, scent, death proximity, and hidden creatures in the mine — which gives future episodes a usable rulebook rather than random scares.
strengths.evidence: The canaries, the full moon, the silver mirror, the sage, the amulet, and the mine gas explanation all function as story rules.

strengths.what_it_means: The frontier setting is familiar enough to orient audiences quickly, but the supernatural overlay makes it feel fresh. That combination is useful for buyers looking for a recognizable world with a differentiating hook.
strengths.evidence: Wyoming mining towns, cattle drives, bounty hunters, and frontier mansions are all grounded in a period audience can immediately picture.

whats_special.headline: WICKED WYOMING is a ferocious supernatural western with a clear series engine: a frontier town built on blood, gold, and hidden monsters. It has the kind of mythic scale, actor-ready roles, and trailer-friendly set pieces that can turn a niche premise into a durable genre series.

lead_characters.name: Abraham Arbuckle
lead_characters.hook: Abraham is the emotional center of the pilot: a stubborn, spiritually anxious man whose decency is constantly colliding with violence, grief, and survival. He begins as the more vulnerable twin in the opening sequence, then grows into a frontier husband and father whose moral certainty is always under pressure. He’s the kind of character who can carry both tenderness and brutality, which makes him feel alive rather than symbolic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a showcase for an actor who can play internal conflict without losing authority. Abraham gets the full range: fear, grief, resolve, rage, and the terrible burden of making choices that cost other people their lives. The role lives in the same performance space as a young Daniel Day-Lewis in There Will Be Blood or a Josh Brolin-type frontier intensity, with enough emotional volatility to anchor a series.

lead_characters.name: Jane Flint Arbuckle
lead_characters.hook: Jane is the pilot’s most dramatic transformation engine: intelligent, observant, and initially trying to hold a family together inside a world of male power games. She carries fear with composure, then earns a ferocious survival turn that makes her the most dangerous person in the final stretch. She’s not ornamental; she’s the one who sees the cost, absorbs the shock, and emerges changed.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a premium dramatic role because it gives an actor a full arc from domestic pressure to blood-soaked agency. The final movement — wounded, hunted, then forced into predatory survival — is the kind of material that can produce a career-making turn. It has the emotional and physical scope of performances like Carrie Coon in The Leftovers or Jodie Comer in Killing Eve, but in a frontier register.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Arbuckle
lead_characters.hook: Jacob is the colder, more certain twin: disciplined, strategic, and deeply invested in the mine as both power base and moral proving ground. He speaks like a man who has already made peace with the devil, which makes him fascinating because he never reads as passive. Even when he’s not physically present, his choices shape the town’s fate.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong authority role for an actor who can play intelligence as menace. Jacob gets to be the man everyone fears, the brother everyone resents, and the believer whose certainty may be its own form of corruption. It has the controlled, dangerous energy of a Michael Shannon or a Matthew Rhys type of part.

lead_characters.name: Buddy Davenport
lead_characters.hook: Buddy is the series’ most unnerving power figure: polished, devout, theatrical, and completely comfortable using manners as a weapon. He can host a dinner, quote history, self-flagellate, and then reveal a predator’s appetite without changing his temperature. He’s a villain with social grace, which makes him especially potent in a serialized world.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is an actor’s part because it lets someone weaponize charm, intelligence, and religious fervor in the same scene. Buddy has the kind of layered menace that can dominate a room and then turn monstrous, giving the performer a chance to play seduction, authority, and horror. It sits comfortably in the territory of a Bryan Cranston or Michael Emerson-style transformation role.

lead_characters.name: Zoma / Burt Mulhollen
lead_characters.hook: Zoma is the show’s wild card: a bounty hunter with a cocky grin, a deadpan sense of humor, and a body that seems to belong to more than one man. He’s funny, cruel, seductive, and impossible to pin down, which makes him feel like a frontier myth walking around in a hat. He gives the series a volatile, charismatic engine that can surprise the audience every time he appears.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role actors chase because it’s both cool and dangerous, with a built-in mystery and a physical transformation hook. The part offers swagger, menace, and a supernatural identity reveal that can evolve over time. It has the same kind of scene-stealing energy as a Walton Goggins or Tom Hardy type of performance space.

considerations.detail: The pilot sits in a mid-to-upper premium genre budget lane because of creature work, period western production design, large-scale death sequences, and multiple night exteriors.
The episode engine is strongly serialized, with the mine, the town power structure, and the vampire mythology all feeding a continuing conflict rather than a case-of-the-week format.
The spider attack, the cavern entity, regenerative vampire wounds, and the bird-fall event all invite a mix of practical effects, makeup, and digital augmentation.
The script includes twins, triplets, children, and multiple roles with specific ethnic and language requirements, which makes ensemble casting a meaningful part of the production plan.
The 1848/1868 frontier setting asks for a strong period design approach across costumes, weapons, transportation, mining infrastructure, and town architecture.
The material is firmly in mature territory, with graphic violence, blood drinking, body horror, and sexualized menace shaping the audience expectation.
